Where it began

Geoff Marsh was born in Northam, Western Australia, on 31 December 1958, and went to Hale School. He was a teenager when he first played for Western Australia, in the Sheffield Shield season of 1977–1978. In 1978 he also turned out five times for South Fremantle at Australian rules football, before deciding that cricket was the game for him.

His first appearance for his state did not go to plan: he was out first ball in both innings at the Sydney Cricket Ground, a feat recorded by hand in the visitors' dressing room for later teams to admire. He took it in his stride and kept knocking on the door of the national side.

The player

His Test debut came against India at Adelaide in December 1985. He played 50 Tests between 1985 and 1992, making 2,854 runs at 33.19 with four hundreds and 15 fifties, and held 38 catches. His highest Test score was 138 against England at Nottingham in 1989.

He opened alongside Mark Taylor and David Boon, and in one-day cricket he was a fixture. With Boon he formed the first Australian opening pair to both make hundreds in the same one-day innings. At the 1987 World Cup in India, which Australia won for the first time, he made 126 not out against New Zealand in Chandigarh.

What made him special

He was a steady, sound right-hander and a good fielder, the kind of opener who did the hard work so that the stroke-makers could follow. Speed was never really his thing, and a modern opener would get through the overs rather more briskly. But he could bat a very long time when he chose: his unbeaten 355 against South Australia in 1989 was one of the highest scores ever made by an Australian in first-class cricket.

In all first-class cricket he made 33 hundreds. He also captained Australia in four one-day internationals and won three of them.

Away from the middle

After retiring in 1994 he became a coach, and in 1996 Australia put him in charge of the national team. Three years later his side won the 1999 World Cup in England with a run of seven straight wins. He went on to serve as a national selector and to coach Zimbabwe from 2001 to 2004, the Pune Warriors in the Indian Premier League, and Sri Lanka in 2011–12. In 2009 he also took charge at Fremantle, the club where he had spent most of his playing days.

And finally

His sons Shaun and Mitchell went on to play Test cricket for Australia, which made him only the third Test cricketer to have two sons do so. Whatever was said at the family dinner table, it seems to have worked.
